sentence: It reaches its top speed almost at once.
claim: A falling raindrop reaches 99% of its terminal velocity within about the first 1% of its fall distance and 5% of its fall time (for even the largest stable drops, in the paper's calculation).
source_title: Loftus and Wordsworth, 'The Physics of Falling Raindrops in Diverse Planetary Atmospheres', arXiv:2102.09570 (full text read, 9 Nov 2026)
note: SOURCE-READ (builder read the arXiv full text; a person has not opened it). Quote: "even the largest possible stable raindrops (described in section 3.4) with the longest acceleration timescales reach 99% of their terminal velocity after starting from rest within the first 1% of their total fall distance and 5% of their total fall time". The film says "almost at once"; the figures are the paper's calculation, not a measurement.

sentence: The faster the drop falls, the harder the air pushes.
claim: The drag force on a falling drop grows with its speed (as the square of the speed).
source_title: Loftus and Wordsworth, 'The Physics of Falling Raindrops in Diverse Planetary Atmospheres', arXiv:2102.09570 (full text read, 9 Nov 2026); also OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, 6.4 (read)
note: SOURCE-READ (builder read the arXiv full text and OpenStax 6.4; a person has not opened them). Paper, Eq. 4: "Drag force on a raindrop is Fdrag = (1/2) CD A rho_air v^2" with v the fall speed relative to air; OpenStax: "Since F_D is proportional to the speed squared".

sentence: At some speed, the push of the air matches the drop's weight.
claim: The terminal velocity is the speed at which the drag force equals the weight.
source_title: Loftus and Wordsworth, 'The Physics of Falling Raindrops in Diverse Planetary Atmospheres', arXiv:2102.09570 (full text read, 9 Nov 2026)
note: SOURCE-READ (builder read the arXiv full text; a person has not opened it). Quote: "the maximum velocity relative to air of a raindrop falling in isolation is its terminal velocity (where Fdrag = Fg)". OpenStax 6.4 says the same for a skydiver (m g = F_D).

sentence: After that, the speed stays the same.
claim: At terminal velocity the net force is zero, so the speed stays constant.
source_title: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, 6.4 'Drag Force and Terminal Speed' (read, 9 Nov 2026)
note: SOURCE-READ (builder read OpenStax 6.4; a person has not opened it). Quote: "At the terminal velocity, F_net = m g - F_D = m a = 0." (the acceleration is zero); the skydiver 'has reached his terminal velocity'.

sentence: Big drops fall faster than small ones.
claim: Raindrop terminal velocity increases with raindrop size.
source_title: Loftus and Wordsworth, 'The Physics of Falling Raindrops in Diverse Planetary Atmospheres', arXiv:2102.09570 (full text read, 9 Nov 2026)
note: SOURCE-READ (builder read the arXiv full text; a person has not opened it). Quote: "raindrop velocity is a monotonically increasing function with raindrop size".

claim: Falling raindrops are never teardrop shaped: they go from spheres to oblate spheroids to shapes like the top of a hamburger bun as they grow.
source_title: Loftus and Wordsworth, 'The Physics of Falling Raindrops in Diverse Planetary Atmospheres', arXiv:2102.09570 (full text read, 9 Nov 2026)
note: SOURCE-READ (builder read the arXiv full text; a person has not opened it). Quote: "Falling raindrops adopt a range of shapes depending on their size—though never the teardrop shape inscribed in the public imagination"; "they evolve from spheres to oblate spheroids to shapes resembling the top of a hamburger bun".

sentence: Small ones are round, and the biggest flatten like a bun, and then break apart.
claim: The largest raindrops flatten to a hamburger-bun shape, and raindrops cannot grow past a size at which they rapidly break apart.
source_title: Loftus and Wordsworth, 'The Physics of Falling Raindrops in Diverse Planetary Atmospheres', arXiv:2102.09570 (full text read, 9 Nov 2026)
note: SOURCE-READ (builder read the arXiv full text; a person has not opened it). Quotes: "shapes resembling the top of a hamburger bun"; "Raindrops cannot grow to infinitely large sizes ... When surface tension ceases to be the dominant force experienced by a raindrop, the raindrop rapidly breaks apart." The picture of the split is an illustration.

sentence: Measure it: in this model, a one-millimeter drop tops out near five meters a second.
claim: In our model (a round drop, drag coefficient 0.5, air density 1.21 kg/m^3), a 1 mm drop's terminal speed is about 4.6 m/s.
source_title: Our own model (compile.py, scene.mjs): v_T = sqrt(2 m g / (rho C A)), the OpenStax 6.4 formula
note: OWN MODEL, OPEN: v_T = sqrt(8 rho_w g r / (3 rho_air C)) for a sphere of radius r: r = 0.5 mm gives 4.6 m/s. Real drops are not spheres and C changes with speed, so real speeds differ; the film badges it as a model. A person should recompute.

claim: In our model, a 5 mm round drop's terminal speed is about 10 m/s.
source_title: Our own model (compile.py, scene.mjs): v_T = sqrt(2 m g / (rho C A)), the OpenStax 6.4 formula
note: OWN MODEL, OPEN: r = 2.5 mm gives 10.4 m/s with C = 0.5. Real drops that big flatten and break apart (c7); the number is the model's, not a measurement. A person should recompute.

sentence: The air gives every drop a speed limit.
claim: A falling raindrop has a terminal velocity (a speed limit set by the air's drag balancing its weight).
source_title: Loftus and Wordsworth, 'The Physics of Falling Raindrops in Diverse Planetary Atmospheres', arXiv:2102.09570 (full text read, 9 Nov 2026)
